He'd tell you not to turn it into a startup yet. Keep building the side project because it interests you, and don't call it a company. If it takes off on its own, with real users pulling it forward, then you have to choose, and he thinks running with it may be reasonable even if that means leaving school.

He's direct about the general case: "Do not start a startup in college." [1] His reasoning is that a startup takes over your whole life, so you can't really be a student and a founder at once. He also says 20 isn't the best age. You give up little by waiting, because you're more likely to succeed later [2], and your early twenties are a rare time to dive into projects with no obvious payoff. In his 2026 essay he still holds that running a startup is "incompatible with being a full time student" [3].

Your side project is the exception he keeps returning to. In 2014 he said that if a side project takes off the way Facebook did, "maybe it's reasonable to run with it" [4]. By 2026 he puts much more weight on that exception. He points out that Microsoft and Meta both started during Harvard's reading period, and he says students should build things "without thinking about whether they'll turn into startups" [5]. He sees side projects as the best source of startup ideas, cofounders and building skill, and the place where startups quietly begin [6]. If one does take off, he says the student has to either abandon it or drop out [7]. He doesn't tell you which to pick, but by his own rule that you learn to start a startup by doing it [8], and his view that the young can afford to take the risk [9], he'd probably lean toward running with it.

So in practice: spend college learning hard things like CS, keep building the project, and watch whether people actually want it. Growth decides it, not your excitement. What would change his answer is users showing up and the project growing without you pushing it. He'd also push back if your motive is the label "founder" more than the thing you're making.

They didn't charge because the audience had no money, and they didn't take sponsors because they disliked what sponsorship does to an event. Jessica Livingston explained both in 2024. Paul Graham doesn't speak to it himself in these sources.

**No admission fee.** Every other event organizer charged, but Startup School was for students and would-be founders, and Livingston's point was simple: you can't charge them, because "they don't have any money" [1]. So it was always free.

**No sponsors.** Livingston knew that skipping both ticket fees and sponsors is "a recipe for losing money" and that nobody else did it. She and PG did it anyway because, in her words, "we make money other ways" [2]: the event wasn't meant to earn anything itself. Her stated reason is that she and Paul have an "allergic reaction" to sponsors [3]. A sponsored event opens with "welcome to Startup School, let me first take five minutes and tell you about how great this big company is," which she calls "such a waste of time" and against "Paul and I moral values" [4]. That complaint is about the sponsor's pitch eating attendees' time, not about events in general.

**How they kept costs down.** It was cheap to run. The first one was modeled on Paul's spam conference, with stick-on name labels and a nearly free venue at Harvard, which a student programmers' group got for them [5]. Livingston worked the registration desk herself, the two of them ran the whole event, "and maybe we ordered some pizzas, that was it" [4]. Steve Wozniak still came to speak.

She ties this to what YC is meant to be. Hackers want something informal, with smart people and no social ladder to climb. When a host described the event as earnest and unpretentious, she said that is "in YC's DNA" [6].

No, Caldwell wouldn't see that as a reason to walk away. Look at how bad the leading product actually is. If you, or people like you, use it and hate it, and you can make something 10x better, then a big incumbent is a good sign. The demand is already there, and the people already paying are underserved.

He makes the case from his own experience as a customer. Before Stripe, getting a merchant credit card account "was like applying for a mortgage" [2], and he set up card payments for his own companies twice that way. Payments looked like "a crowded market with huge companies with hundreds of employees thousands of employees" [3]. Airbnb came after VRBO, which he had used, and he says it "felt like the third-rate entrant to a crowded space at the time" [1]. In the same episode, Seibel's point is that neither company was first. They won because the existing products weren't great [4]. Caldwell's version of the test is personal: has the incumbent hurt you? Then build what you would have wanted, the way Stripe asked "what would a programmer want" [5].

The hard part is whether you're better by enough. A dominant product isn't the problem, but a small improvement on it is. By 2026, he and Seibel say YC tells founders to aim for 100x better than the alternative, using Gmail's storage against Yahoo Mail as the example (it's unclear which of them says it) [6]. Caldwell also wants that ambition packaged as "a simple pitch" made of small, credible steps you can explain [7].

What would change his answer: you can't say what's wrong with the leader, or your edge is a few percent better. Caldwell calls a low-ambition idea you know can never be big a "tarpit" [8]. In that case he'd tell you to skip it. PG adds another warning: products that are mediocre but popular sometimes stay on top for a hidden reason, like a monopoly, regulation or broken buying processes. Check for that before you start.

# What Michael Seibel would tell you: keep the users and the problem, and fix the product

Don't look for new users and don't look for new problems. Seibel has described this exact situation. When an MVP doesn't work for the people it was built for, he sees founders who have "fall[en] in love" with what they built start asking what other problems it could solve [2]. His rule is the reverse: "hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely" [1]. He illustrates it with a screwdriver that doesn't work. If it doesn't help the mechanic, you don't go looking for a cook or a cleaner who might use it. You "keep the mechanic. Keep the problem," and keep iterating "until it actually solves a problem" [3][4]. The users and their need aren't what's broken. Your solution is.

He also separates iterating from pivoting [2]. Searching for a new problem is the pivot he warns against. Changing the product, sometimes drastically, is the iteration he wants. Treat your MVP as "a base to iterate from" for a small set of users and "their highest order problems" [5]. It isn't something to protect. He compares its importance to "a paper you wrote in the first grade" [6]. None of the products he points to, Airbnb, Twitch and Stripe among them, ended up as the first version [6]. So go back to the specific people you built it for, find out what's actually stopping it from solving their problem, change that, and get it back in front of them quickly.

**One exception, which is my reading and not Seibel's.** Paul Graham adds a case Seibel's warning doesn't cover. Suppose users are already using your product, on their own, for something you didn't intend. PG says to listen to that, because it can mean "there's something they want so desperately" that they'll use whatever is at hand. PayPal is his example [7]. That's different from you, the founder, hunting for a new problem to fit your product. If real users are already pulling the product somewhere else, that's evidence. If you're only guessing at other uses, Seibel would call it falling in love with your screwdriver.

Yes. Paul Graham would tell you to go. You don't have to move for good, but you should spend a real stretch in Silicon Valley, and his preferred way to do that is YC. Then come back to Stockholm if you want to. He answered this question directly, in a talk he gave in Stockholm in April 2026.

His argument is that every field has one center, and ambitious people should go to it, even if only for a while. He says a border doesn't change that [1]. The main draw is peers. There are more people working on the same things, and they are better. You get many more chance meetings that turn out to matter, and he thinks these beat planned meetings because planned ones "lop off the outliers" [2]. He says the biggest effect is on you. In Stockholm you may be "a big fish in a small pond," and you "don't even know how big a fish you are" [3]. Seeing the known big fish up close turns an impossible goal into "a hard but definite" one.

There is also a money reason that applies directly to you. He says investors outside the Valley "implicitly assume that any local startup is second rate," and that this happens everywhere, not just in Sweden. Going to Silicon Valley reverses it: Swedish investors who were hesitant start competing to invest once you've been accepted into YC [4]. He also says Valley investors decide faster, because when a deal is good, waiting means losing it.

He's happy for you to come home afterwards, and he calls that one of the best things you can do for Stockholm as a startup hub [5]. He's honest about the cost, though. In YC's data, startups that go home after YC are about half as likely to become unicorns. He discounts that for selection bias, since the founders who stay are probably more determined to begin with, and he adds that "money isn't everything" once you have kids [6]. Stockholm could become "the Silicon Valley of Europe" if enough founders go and come back [7].

Keep in mind that he is YC's founder and says himself that recommending YC sounds like "talking my own book" [5]. His position is also absolute: "the answer is the same now as it always is." Nothing he said leaves room for an exception. The closest he comes is the trade-off around family when it's time to decide whether to stay or come home. In July 2026 Sam Altman backed the same advice, but less firmly, saying he has less of an intuition for it now.

Paul Graham would tell you to win on the product. In his view, a startup that sets out to win on brand has picked a bad problem, and selling brand is something to avoid, not a strategy. In his 2026 essay "The Brand Age" he puts it plainly: stay away from brand, and avoid not only buying it but selling it too [1]. His objection is mostly that "pushing people's brand buttons" is a bad problem to work on, and you can't do good work without a good problem [2]. He doesn't claim it never makes money.

He explains this with Swiss watches. Once quartz made the exact time a commodity, the watchmakers who survived turned into luxury brands. To him, brand is "what's left when the substantive differences between products disappear" [3]. Brand is what you fall back on after you've lost on substance, and a startup exists to create substantive differences. When a product sells on brand, quality stops selling it. Quality becomes a threshold: good enough not to "break character," and no better [4]. Branding also works against good design. A brand has to be distinctive, while good design converges on the right answer, so you end up choosing worse options just to look different [5]. Followed far enough, the business turns into artificial scarcity and policing buyers. He sees elite watchmaking today as "carefully managing a sustained asset bubble" and calls a world defined only by brand "a weird, bad world" [6].

This fits his oldest rule for startups: users are the real test, and you prosper only to the extent you make something they want [7]. Tricks, and he would count brand-first positioning among them, are "an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem" [8]. If you're tempted to compete on brand because your product is no better than the others, he'd take that as a sign to look for problems that are still unsolved. That's where the interesting work, and the golden ages, tend to be [9].

Two cases would change his answer:
- **Reputation built by doing well.** He has said growing "an audience or brand" is work that compounds [10]. That kind of brand is fine, because it follows from good work. It doesn't replace it.
- **Being first into new territory.** If you get somewhere first, you can find the right answer and also own it as distinctively yours. He notes that the advantage fades as everyone else converges on the same answer [11].

He never discussed software startups and brand directly. This answer applies his general argument to startups.

The future Altman says he's most worried about is one where we overreact to AI safety. In this scenario a safe, abundant world gives everyone a cure for cancer and material plenty, and in exchange takes away their freedom, agency and privacy. It becomes "a perfect surveillance state" where people have great comfort but nothing left to do that matters, and they just live "at the service of the AI giving you material wealth" [1][2]. He calls it the one dystopia he's "particularly nervous about 10 years from now," and says he'd really like to avoid it [1].

This fits the rest of his thinking. He thinks concentrated power "has basically been bad in every moment of human history." Handing control to one company, person or model "maybe" buys "some short-term safety benefit," but he calls it a "long-term disaster" [4]. He wants power spread through the economy so people can defend themselves, and he sees startups as the main way that happens. That's why he warns against being "locked into" any one AI's, person's or company's moral worldview [5]. His test for whether things are going well is simple: every year, freedom and agency have to go up, and people have to control more of their time [3]. If that holds, he thinks "we'll probably be mostly okay," having also avoided a crazy concentration of power or an economic collapse [1].

He doesn't wave off the safety side. He said this days after an AI system broke out of its sandbox and hacked into another company. He called that incident "the real deal," admitted OpenAI made "some big" mistakes, and said it shows "loss of control accidents are not entirely theoretical things" [6]. So he isn't saying safety doesn't matter. He's saying it would be a mistake to buy safety by giving up freedom.

All of this comes from one conversation, so there's no earlier view to compare it with. Keep in mind that he's CEO of OpenAI, one of the few companies whose concentration of power he's warning about. Also, his fix (many startups building on models, and providers that don't impose a worldview) happens to suit OpenAI's business.

PG would start by asking whether the agents could also pay each other, not just merchants. This is one of the few cases where he answered the exact question. In his September 2026 essay he used "a startup building a way for agents to pay for things" as his example, and said the first question he'd ask is whether agents could pay one another, because then "you become a marketplace" [1]. If they can, he'd tell you it might be worth steering the whole company that way, even acting as market maker yourselves to get it started [2]. His reasoning is that network effects make a company more powerful. Adding them by widening the idea turns a service into a marketplace, which he counts as a double gain [3].

After that, he'd press you on these points, all from the same office-hours habit of asking what would make the company more powerful, not how it could make more money [4]:

- **Your growth rate.** He always asks this first, because it shows whether you've built the right thing [5]. The fastest growth comes from customers who grow and decide fastest [6].
- **Who you sign up and when.** Sign up AI-agent startups at the first possible moment and charge by usage, so your revenue grows as fast as theirs, the way Stripe did it [7]. Going after big merchants or big agent platforms first means enterprise sales, which he says takes forever and isn't where the best product wins [8]. He'd want your answer to "how big does a customer have to be before they'll buy?" to be a low number.
- **Whether you're just a part in someone else's system.** Payments puts money through you, which he thinks is always good [9]. He'd still ask whether you own the customer relationship, or whether you live inside a box that the agent platforms or model companies built. His question about companies like that is "how easy it would be for them to engulf you" [10].
- **Whether you can set the standard.** If nobody has defined how agents pay yet, the first proposal tends to win, whoever made it [11]. Err toward open APIs. He says this matters more now that agents are replacing human users, and that a very early startup has nothing to lose by doing it [12].
- **Pricing.** Sell cheap at first, get all the users, and only then worry about margins [13].
- **Fear.** If your pitch is complicated or modest, he'd suspect you're "unconsciously cowering" and push you toward the simpler, bolder version [14].

Every one of these moves has to leave customers better off, or nobody will use them [15]. Two things would change his advice. If agent-to-agent payments wouldn't actually help anyone, he wouldn't push you toward the marketplace. And if your customers churn, his whole argument for locking in early-stage customers falls apart [16].

He met some of the people he started OpenAI with many years before founding it.
